Accounting demand is seasonal and referral-led, and the firms that grow are the ones visible in the weeks before each deadline.
Architecture is chosen on portfolio and on the client's belief that the practice will understand what they actually want.
Vehicle buyers research online for weeks and visit once, which makes the pre-visit content the actual showroom.
A B2B service sale is a decision about risk, made by someone whose reputation is attached to the outcome.
Salons are booked on visual proof and rebooked on habit, which makes portfolio content and rebooking sequences the two things that matter.
Childcare is chosen on trust and proximity, researched anxiously and decided after a visit, which makes the visit the conversion event.
Independent coaches sell their own judgement, which means visibility and credibility are the same problem and both rest on one person.
Construction is sold on evidence of finished work and on the buyer's confidence that you will turn up and finish.
Consulting is sold on a point of view, and a firm without a stated one competes only on rate card.
A creator's audience is the asset, and the business fails when audience growth is optimised at the expense of the offer that monetises it.
Security marketing has to create urgency without trading on fear, which is a narrow path most of the category fails to walk.
Dentistry combines routine local demand with high-value elective treatment, and the two need entirely different marketing.
Driving instruction is a local, referral-heavy purchase where availability and pass evidence carry the decision.
Ecommerce lives or dies on the economics of acquisition and repeat purchase, and content is what makes both survivable.
EdTech sells to institutions with budget cycles and to individuals with immediate needs, and the two motions share almost nothing.
Education is bought on outcome and trust, at a moment determined by an intake date rather than by marketing.
Conference sales are a race against a fixed date with three separate audiences — attendees, speakers and sponsors — each needing different persuasion.
Event businesses sell an outcome that cannot be sampled, to a buyer who will make the decision once and cannot afford to get it wrong.
Financial advice is bought from a person, but found through a firm, which means both need to be visible and consistent.
Fintech marketing carries a regulatory weight most consumer marketing does not, and the compliance review is part of the production process rather than a check at the end.
Fitness businesses acquire in bursts and lose members quietly, which makes retention content more valuable than acquisition content.
Food brands are bought on appetite and repeat, which makes visual content and sampling the two levers that actually move volume.
Healthcare marketing is constrained by regulation and by the fact that the reader is often worried, which makes clarity and restraint more effective than persuasion.
Home services demand is urgent, local and largely decided by who answers first with a clear price and a clear time.
Hospitality is booked after comparison across channels you do not control, which makes direct booking content the highest-value work available.
HR consulting is bought when something has gone wrong or a regulation has changed, which makes topical authority the main acquisition mechanism.
Insurance is bought reluctantly and renewed automatically, so most marketing effort is best spent on the renewal window and on the moments that trigger a new policy.
Interior design is discovered visually and bought on trust in taste, which means the visual channels generate the lead and the written content closes it.
Managed IT is bought after a failure, which means marketing has to be present before the failure and specific about response times.
Legal enquiries arrive at a moment of stress, and the firm that is findable, clear and quick to respond usually wins regardless of relative expertise.
Local retail competes with online convenience, and wins on immediacy, curation and being part of a place.
Logistics is bought on reliability and switched over failure, which makes marketing a matter of demonstrating operational control.
Industrial buyers are technical, specification-driven and searching for a solution to a defined engineering problem.
Agencies market themselves last, which is visible to prospects and is usually the reason the pipeline is inconsistent.
A marketplace has to market to both sides at once, and the side that is scarce changes as the platform grows.
Aesthetic treatments sit between healthcare and beauty, which means the marketing has to convert on visual proof while staying inside medical advertising rules.
Membership organisations are judged annually at renewal, which makes continuous demonstration of value the whole marketing job.
Therapy is sought at a low point, and the marketing that works is the marketing that reduces the effort required to make first contact.
Nonprofits market to two audiences with opposite needs — funders who want evidence and supporters who want a story — usually with no marketing budget at all.
Professional services are bought on trust in a specific person's judgement, which is difficult to scale and easy to erode with generic marketing.
Property management is won on operational credibility and lost on responsiveness, which makes the marketing argument almost entirely about process.
Property is a high-value, infrequent purchase where the agent is chosen on local credibility and responsiveness rather than on marketing polish.
Recruitment is a two-sided market, and most agencies market to clients while neglecting the candidate side that actually constrains delivery.
Restaurants are chosen in the last twenty minutes before a decision, which makes discoverability and current information more valuable than brand building.
Software buyers self-educate for weeks before they contact anyone, so most of the selling happens in content you are not present for.
Subscription commerce is a retention business wearing an acquisition business's clothes, and the churn curve decides everything.
Travel is researched extensively and booked emotionally, which means content has to do the practical reassurance and the desire in the same piece.
Tutoring is bought by a parent under time pressure, on the basis of trust in the tutor and evidence that the approach works.
Veterinary clients are emotionally invested and cost-sensitive at the same time, which makes transparency about price the central marketing problem.

Above the fold is the portion of a page visible before any scrolling, which now varies enormously by device.
An asset format is a defined content structure with its own anatomy, length rules and success conditions.
Attribution is the practice of assigning credit for a conversion to the marketing touches that contributed to it.
Segmentation is splitting your market into groups that require genuinely different messages.
Bottom-of-funnel content addresses someone ready to decide, and removes the last reasons not to.
Brand voice is the consistent set of language choices that make content recognisably from one business.
The buyer journey is the sequence of states a customer passes through from not knowing they have a problem to having chosen a solution.
The buying cycle is the elapsed time between a buyer first recognising a need and making a decision.
A call to action is the specific next step a piece of content asks the reader to take.
A campaign is a bounded marketing effort with a defined offer, audience, window and end condition.
A campaign theme is the single argument a business makes across a defined period.
A canonical URL tells search engines which version of a page is the definitive one.
Channel strategy is the decision about which platforms you will invest in and, more importantly, which you will not.
Churn rate is the proportion of customers who stop buying or subscribing in a given period.
Click-through rate is the proportion of people who saw something and clicked it.
A content calendar assigns what will be published, where and when, ahead of time.
A content pillar is a recurring subject area that a business publishes on consistently.
Repurposing is re-expressing one idea across several formats and platforms.
Conversion rate is the proportion of people at one step who reach the next one.
Core Web Vitals are a set of measurements of loading speed, interaction responsiveness and layout stability.
Creative fatigue is the decline in performance that occurs as an audience sees the same advertising creative repeatedly.
Customer acquisition cost is total sales and marketing spend divided by the number of customers it produced.
Customer lifetime value is the total profit a customer generates across the whole relationship.
Onboarding is the guided path from purchase to a customer's first real result.
Deliverability is whether your email reaches the inbox rather than the spam folder or nowhere at all.
Double opt-in requires a subscriber to confirm their address before receiving anything, usually via a confirmation email.
A drip campaign is a series of messages sent automatically on a fixed schedule after a trigger.
An editorial calendar plans content by theme and argument rather than by publication date.
An editorial guardrail is a rule that constrains what generated content is permitted to claim or say.
Engagement rate is the proportion of people who saw content and interacted with it in some way.
Evergreen content stays useful and accurate long after publication, which makes it the only content that keeps earning rather than expiring.
First-touch attribution credits the entire conversion to the first marketing interaction a customer had.
A funnel is the sequence of steps between first contact and purchase, with a measurable drop-off at each one.
A hook is the opening line or frame that determines whether anyone consumes the rest of an asset.
An ideal customer profile describes the type of buyer your offer serves best, defined by situation and need rather than by demographics.
Impression share is the proportion of available impressions your advertising actually received.
Intent segmentation groups contacts by what they have actually done rather than by where they came from.
Internal linking connects related pages on your own site to each other.
A landing page is a page built around a single decision, usually the destination of a campaign or an ad.
Last-touch attribution credits the conversion entirely to the final interaction before purchase.
A lead magnet is something valuable enough that someone will exchange contact details for it.
Lead nurturing is the structured follow-up that carries someone from first contact to a decision.
Lead scoring ranks contacts by how likely they are to buy, based on the actions they have taken.
List hygiene is the practice of suppressing and removing contacts who no longer engage.
A location page is a page targeting a specific geography you serve, with content genuinely specific to it.
A long-tail keyword is a longer, more specific query with lower volume and usually higher intent.
A lookalike audience is a targeting group built by a platform to resemble an audience you supply.
A marketing experiment is a deliberate change made with a stated expectation and a defined window.
The marketing mix is the combination of channels, offers and messages a business uses to reach its market.
A marketing qualified lead is a contact whose behaviour suggests they are worth a sales conversation.
A meta description is the short summary a search engine may show beneath your page title in results.
Middle-of-funnel content addresses people actively evaluating approaches and comparing options.
A minimum viable audience is the smallest group of people who could sustain the business if you served them well.
Objection handling is addressing the specific reasons a buyer has not to proceed, directly and in advance.
An offer ladder is the sequence of increasing commitments a customer can make, from free to core paid offer.
Open rate is the proportion of delivered emails that were recorded as opened.
Payback period is how long it takes for a customer to generate enough profit to cover what it cost to acquire them.
Positioning is the claim your business makes about what it is for and who it is for, expressed so a customer could repeat it.
A promotional calendar plans when offers are made and to whom, across a year.
A re-engagement campaign contacts people who have stopped opening or responding, and asks them to stay or go.
Retargeting shows advertising to people who have already visited your site or engaged with your content.
The sales cycle is the time from a qualified enquiry to a closed decision, measured from your side of the conversation.
A sales qualified lead is a contact that sales has accepted as a genuine opportunity after a conversation.
Schema markup is structured data added to a page so search engines can understand what it describes.
Search intent is what a person is actually trying to accomplish when they type a query.
Seasonality is the predictable variation in demand across a year for a particular business.
Social proof is evidence that other people have already chosen you — reviews, testimonials, usage or recognisable customers.
Tone of voice is how the brand voice adapts to a specific context — an apology, a launch, a support reply.
Top-of-funnel content addresses people who have the problem but are not yet looking for a solution.
A value proposition states the specific outcome a customer gets and what makes it different from the alternatives available to them.
Watch-through rate is the proportion of a video an average viewer watches before leaving.
A welcome sequence is the set of messages a new subscriber receives immediately after joining.
